protocol.what_baseline_fairness_did: baseline_fairness listed the grids (hyperparams.csv, 72 rows) and asserted 'classical tuned at least as hard as quantum on the SVM axis' in prose, quoting CV-only fit counts (rbf_svm 16/80, random_forest 4/20, mlp 4/20, xgboost 36/180, quantum 20); it never gave a per-model budget table, never counted the refit, never counted the representation axis, and never measured time.
protocol.reconciliation_with_baseline_fairness: tuning_budget's n_fits_cv_only column reproduces baseline_fairness's quoted numbers exactly (80/20/20/180 and quantum 20); n_fits adds the single refit sklearn performs after the search (refit=True default).
protocol.n_configs_source: INTROSPECTED: build_baseline(name, configs/baselines.yaml, seed=17, folds=5, tune=True).param_grid expanded with sklearn.model_selection.ParameterGrid -- so the two code-truths baseline_fairness documented are picked up automatically (XGBoost's grid is a code default; MLP early_stopping is hard-coded False in the binary path).
protocol.n_gradient_steps_definition: parameter-update steps spent learning a REPRESENTATION; 0 for kernel/tree/neighbour models; per-model basis in the gradient_steps_basis column
protocol.n_trainable_params_definition: quantum feature-map parameters actually optimised, counted from the live CrossLayerFeatureMap object (fm.init_params() element counts), with the inert (L,1) gamma tensor of the zero-coupling map excluded

wall_clock_provenance.reason: results/packetloss_dev/{summary,provenance}.json record only one aggregate wall_time_s = 858.5 s for the entire packet-loss sweep (11 loss levels x 8 model rows + 200-replicate grouped bootstraps); no per-model timer is written anywhere in the Table-I pipeline, and no other artefact under results/ carries per-model timing for these models.
wall_clock_provenance.tuning_budget_measurement: re-measured here on the matched-N protocol in three flavours: measured_tuning_wall_s (as-shipped, parallelism on), measured_tuning_cpu_s (process-tree CPU via psutil -- getrusage under-counts because loky workers are kept alive, not reaped), and measured_tuning_core_s (SERIAL re-run: joblib n_jobs=1, estimator n_jobs=1, threadpoolctl limit 1, torch.set_num_threads(1)) -- the last is the only timing comparable across models. Machine-dependent; quote as an order of magnitude only.
wall_clock_provenance.cpu_s_caveat: measured_tuning_cpu_s is a process-TREE total and still carries loky overhead (worker poll/teardown) even after the pool warm-up, so it can exceed the serial core-seconds for the same search; cite measured_tuning_core_s, not cpu_s.

fairness_verdict.question: Is any model advantaged by tuning budget?

axis_1_enumerated_classifier_search.unit: model fits = n_configs x cv_folds + 1 refit
axis_1_enumerated_classifier_search.why_rbf_has_more_configs: the QSVM and the RBF-SVM search the SAME 4-value C grid ([0.1, 1.0, 10.0, 100.0]); the RBF-SVM additionally searches 4 kernel bandwidths (['scale', 0.01, 0.1, 1.0]), which the QSVM has no analogue of because its kernel geometry is set by the trained feature map -- hence 16 configs vs 4

low_label_counterexample.evidence: results/lowlabel_dev/lowlabel_results.csv, mean PR-AUC over repeats: ocsvm_classical 0.685 / 0.679 / 0.700 at n_train 50 / 100 / 200 vs qsvm_crosslayer 0.514 / 0.545 / 0.521 (and qsvm_zz 0.279 / 0.332 / 0.319)
low_label_counterexample.reading: this is the ONE classical model that beats the QSVM on a SMALLER tuning budget, and it strengthens rather than weakens the honest finding: the low-label winner is the least-tuned model in the whole zoo, so the low-label advantage belongs to the one-class/anomaly-detection PARADIGM, not to tuning effort and not to quantum kernels (H3 refuted).

axis_1_enumerated_classifier_search.verdict: CLASSICAL >= QUANTUM on the main binary comparison. Each of the three classical comparators that beat the cross-layer QSVM over the three leakage-safe splits was searched at least as hard as it: random_forest 21 fits (1.0x the QSVM's 21), rbf_svm 81 (3.9x), xgboost 181 (8.6x); the MLP matched-N row is also 21 (1.0x), and knn_bagging (16), which was tuned LESS than the QSVM, does not beat it on either dataset (NextGen ROC-AUC 0.880 vs 0.929). So within the headline detection comparison no model that outperforms the QSVM was tuned more weakly than it, and the no-advantage finding is NOT an artefact of an under-tuned classical side -- on this axis the comparison is conservative in the quantum models' favour. The single exception sits OUTSIDE that comparison and cuts the same way: in the low-label regime the classical one-class SVM (4 fits, 0.19x the QSVM budget) beats the cross-layer QSVM by +0.13 to +0.18 PR-AUC at n_train 50-200 -- the least-tuned model in the zoo wins there, which is a paradigm effect, not a budget effect.

axis_2_structural_hyperparameters.unit: number of structural hyperparameters with >1 searched value
axis_2_structural_hyperparameters.verdict: The quantum models searched ZERO structural hyperparameters: n_layers=2, entangler, coupling=full_bipartite, AoI kappa=0.5, and the whole KTA schedule (Adam, lr 0.05, 200 epochs, batch 512, init (1,1,0.5), seed 11) were fixed a priori in configs/quantum.yaml and never tuned, whereas every classical baseline searched 1-4 structural hyperparameters (kernel bandwidth, tree depth/count, hidden-layer sizes, boosting rounds/depth/learning rate/class weight).

axis_3_gradient_trained_representation.verdict: This is the one axis the quantum models get and the kernel/tree/neighbour baselines do not: 200 Adam steps over 64 cross-layer map parameters. It is NOT a quantum-only axis though -- the MLP baseline gradient-trains 2,689-9,473 weights (measured: {'(64, 32)': 2689, '(128, 64)': 9473}) inside every one of its 21 fits, 42x-148x the quantum map's 64 parameters, over 109,200 update steps against the map's 200; the LSTM sequence baseline likewise takes 480 Adam steps. qsvm_zz receives ZERO representation budget by design (fixed_params ablation), so the cross-layer >> ZZ gap is a trained-vs-untrained gap, not a topology gap.

fairness_verdict.paradigm_caveat: KTA tunes the REPRESENTATION by gradient descent on a detector-free alignment objective; classical grids tune the CLASSIFIER by enumeration against cross-validated average precision. No exchange rate between a gradient step and a grid fit is claimed. The comparison above is a comparison of BUDGET in each currency, not a claim of equivalence between the two search paradigms.
fairness_verdict.unit_cost_caveat: One 'fit' is not one learner: a random-forest fit trains 200-500 trees and an XGBoost fit up to 400 boosting rounds, so n_base_learners_total (measured) is the harsher and more honest cost measure -- and it is larger for the classical side by three to four orders of magnitude.

axis_4_measured_wall_clock.unit: seconds of tuning on this machine, matched-N protocol
axis_4_measured_wall_clock.provenance: RE-MEASURED by tuning_budget; the published run's per-model timing is IRRECOVERABLE (see protocol.wall_clock_provenance)
axis_4_measured_wall_clock.timing_noise_note: this machine ran other jobs concurrently; repeat runs of tuning_budget moved the quantum KTA timing by up to ~40% wall / ~13% serial-core, so quote these as approximate orders of magnitude
axis_4_measured_wall_clock.verdict: Time is the axis on which the quantum models cost more, and essentially all of it is KTA feature-map training plus the O(N^2) Gram, NOT hyperparameter search: the cross-layer QSVM's C-grid CV takes 0.81s of its 44.1s. On the parallelism-free comparison (serial, one thread everywhere) the QSVM's whole tuning costs 41.75 core-seconds against 25.4 for the most expensive classical search (mlp), a factor of 1.6. Timings are machine- and load-dependent and should be quoted as orders of magnitude, not as metrics.

headline.fairness_verdict_one_line: On the enumerated-search axis the classical baselines were tuned at least as hard as the quantum models (81 vs 21 fits for RBF-SVM, 181 vs 21 for XGBoost, 21 vs 21 for the random forest, 21 vs 21 for the MLP) and searched 1-4 structural hyperparameters against the quantum models' zero; the quantum models' only extra budget is 200 Adam steps over 64 feature-map parameters, which is itself smaller than the MLP's gradient-trained weight budget; and the one classical model that beats the QSVM on a SMALLER budget (the one-class SVM, 4 fits, in the low-label regime) makes the no-advantage finding stronger, not weaker.
